questions.stem: In a multicellular animal, which sequence runs from the smallest level of organisation to the largest?
options: Tissue, cell, system, organ
Cell, organ, tissue, system
Organ, tissue, cell, system
Cell, tissue, organ, system
questions.explanation: Similar cells form tissues, several tissues form an organ, and organs working together form a system. The stomach, for example, is an organ made of muscle, epithelial and other tissues.

questions.stem: The stomach contains muscle tissue, epithelial tissue and nervous tissue. Why is it classed as an organ?
options: It is made of several tissues working together to carry out a function
It is made of one type of cell repeated many times in the same layer
It is a group of organs that together carry out one main function
It is a single cell that is large enough to be seen without a microscope
questions.explanation: An organ is a structure made of two or more tissues that work together to perform a function. A group of organs working together, such as the whole digestive tract and glands, is a system.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of digestion?
options: To release energy from glucose so that the muscles of the gut can contract
To remove all of the water from food before it passes into the large intestine
To break large food molecules into small ones that can be absorbed into the blood
To build large molecules from small ones so they can be stored in the gut wall
questions.explanation: Large molecules such as starch, proteins and fats are too big to cross the gut wall, so they are broken into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed and used by cells.

questions.stem: Chewing food and the churning of the stomach do not change the chemical nature of food. Why are they important for digestion?
options: They break food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymes
They release enzymes from the food so that it can digest itself in the gut
They raise the temperature of the food to the optimum for the digestive enzymes
They remove the water from food so that enzymes become more concentrated
questions.explanation: Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, giving a larger surface area on which enzymes can act, so chemical digestion is faster. It does not change the molecules themselves.

questions.stem: What is peristalsis?
options: Chemical breakdown of proteins by enzymes in the stomach
Absorption of digested food through the walls of the villi
Grinding of food by the molars before it is swallowed
Waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the wave-like contraction of circular and longitudinal muscles in the gut wall that moves food along. It also mixes food with digestive juices.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a digestive enzyme with its substrate and products is correct?
options: Lipase: lipids to fatty acids and glycerol
Amylase: proteins to amino acids
Protease: starch to maltose and glucose
Lipase: starch to fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. Amylase acts on starch, giving maltose, and protease breaks proteins into peptides and amino acids.

questions.stem: Starch is mixed with saliva in one test tube and with boiled saliva in another, both at 37 °C. After 10 minutes, iodine solution is added. Which result is expected?
options: Both tubes turn blue-black, as saliva has no effect on starch at 37 °C
Neither tube turns blue-black, as boiling greatly speeds up starch digestion
Only the boiled saliva tube turns blue-black, as its amylase is denatured
Only the unboiled saliva tube turns blue-black, as amylase makes starch
questions.explanation: Amylase in active saliva digests the starch, so iodine stays brown. Boiling denatures the amylase, so starch remains and iodine turns blue-black.

questions.stem: Which feature of the villi in the small intestine helps absorb digested food quickly?
options: A thick muscular wall that grinds the food into small pieces
A lining of cilia that sweep the food back into the stomach
A layer of fat that stores glucose before it is absorbed
A wall one cell thick with a dense network of capillaries
questions.explanation: Villi, with microvilli on their cells, give a huge surface area. A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance, and a rich blood supply carries absorbed food away, keeping the concentration gradient steep.

questions.stem: A disease flattens the villi of the small intestine. Which effect is most likely?
options: Mechanical digestion stops, because the villi grind food in the small intestine
Food can no longer be swallowed, because the villi start the process of peristalsis
Less digested food is absorbed, because the surface area for absorption is reduced
More digested food is absorbed, because food moves more slowly past a flat lining
questions.explanation: Villi greatly increase the absorbing surface, so flattening them reduces absorption of nutrients, which can lead to weight loss and deficiencies. Villi do not grind food or cause peristalsis.

questions.stem: Which list shows materials eliminated from the digestive system in faeces?
options: Urea and excess water filtered from the blood by the kidneys
Carbon dioxide produced by cellular respiration in the gut wall cells
Indigestible material such as cellulose, excess materials and some metabolic wastes
Glucose, amino acids and fatty acids that have been absorbed into the blood
questions.explanation: Faeces contain undigested matter such as cellulose (fibre), excess materials and some metabolic wastes, such as bile pigments from the breakdown of haemoglobin. Urea is removed by the kidneys in urine.

questions.stem: Bile contains no enzymes, yet removing the gall bladder can make fatty meals harder to digest. Why?
options: Bile breaks fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase
Bile contains amylase, which helps lipase break down starch and fat
Bile absorbs fatty acids and carries them through the villi into blood
Bile makes the stomach more acidic, which is needed for fat digestion
questions.explanation: Bile, made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, emulsifies fats into small droplets, a physical change that gives lipase a larger surface area to act on. It contains no digestive enzymes.

questions.stem: Which set of features do efficient gas exchange surfaces share?
options: Large surface area, thin, moist and well supplied with blood
Small surface area, thick, dry and well supplied with blood
Large surface area, thick, moist and without blood vessels
Small surface area, thin, dry and without any blood vessels
questions.explanation: A large area and thin barrier increase the rate of diffusion, moisture lets gases dissolve before diffusing, and a good blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep.

questions.stem: Why does a rich blood supply around the alveoli increase the rate of gas exchange?
options: Blood flow makes the alveolar walls thicker so they do not collapse
Blood flow carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide, keeping gradients steep
Blood flow pumps oxygen actively from the alveoli into red blood cells
Blood flow cools the alveoli so that oxygen dissolves less in the moisture
questions.explanation: Blood constantly removes the oxygen that diffuses in and brings more carbon dioxide, so the concentration differences between air and blood stay large. Gas exchange is by diffusion, not active pumping.

questions.stem: Which changes happen during inhalation?
options: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume increases and air pressure in the lungs falls
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, chest volume decreases and air pressure in the lungs rises
The diaphragm contracts and flattens, chest volume decreases and air pressure in the lungs rises
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, chest volume increases and air pressure in the lungs falls
questions.explanation: As the diaphragm contracts and the rib cage moves up and out, the chest volume increases, so the pressure inside the lungs drops below atmospheric pressure and air flows in.

questions.stem: How does breathing help to maintain efficient gas exchange in the alveoli?
options: It moistens the alveoli so that no carbon dioxide can dissolve in them
It increases the thickness of the alveolar walls so that they last longer
It replaces alveolar air, keeping oxygen high and carbon dioxide low in the alveoli
It forces oxygen through the alveolar walls by raising the air pressure
questions.explanation: Ventilation brings in fresh air and removes air rich in carbon dioxide, maintaining the concentration gradients for diffusion. Gases cross the alveolar walls by diffusion, not because they are forced through.

questions.stem: Through which structures do gases mainly enter and leave a leaf?
options: Phloem tubes
Root hairs
Stomata
Xylem vessels
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores, mostly on the underside of the leaf, controlled by guard cells. Gases diffuse through them and the air spaces in the leaf. Xylem and phloem carry water and sugars, not gases.

questions.stem: How does carbon dioxide reach the photosynthesising cells inside a leaf?
options: By being carried in the phloem from the roots up to the leaves and stems
By being dissolved in soil water and carried up in the xylem
By being pumped through the leaf veins by root pressure from below
By diffusion through stomata and air spaces, without using the transport system
questions.explanation: Gases move in plants by diffusion through stomata, air spaces and the plant surface; the plant transport system is not involved. Xylem and phloem carry water, minerals and sugars.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the body through the aorta?
options: Left atrium
Right atrium
Left ventricle
Right ventricle
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and around the body. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: Why does the left ventricle have a much thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle?
options: It must pump blood at higher pressure all around the body
It must hold a much larger volume of blood than the right
It receives blood directly from all of the body's veins
It pumps deoxygenated blood, which is thicker than other blood
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood through the whole body, which needs a higher pressure than pumping to the nearby lungs. Both ventricles pump the same volume of blood with each beat.

questions.stem: Which is the correct path of blood from the body back to the body?
options: Vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, lungs, right atrium, right ventricle, aorta
Pulmonary vein, right atrium, right ventricle, body, left atrium, left ventricle, lungs
Vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta
Aorta, left atrium, left ventricle, lungs, right atrium, right ventricle, vena cava
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right side of the heart and is pumped to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left side and is pumped out through the aorta. This is a double circulation.

questions.stem: What is the function of the valves in the heart?
options: To speed up the heartbeat when the body needs more oxygen
To mix oxygenated and deoxygenated blood before it leaves
To filter out bacteria from the blood as it passes through
To stop blood flowing backwards, keeping flow in one direction
questions.explanation: Valves between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits of the ventricles, close when pressure behind them falls, preventing backflow. The heart rate is set by the pacemaker, not the valves.

questions.stem: Which feature of capillaries makes them suited to exchanging materials with body cells?
options: Valves along their length that prevent blood flowing back
A wide lumen that carries a large volume of blood very quickly
Walls only one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
Thick elastic walls that can withstand high blood pressure
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of thin cells, so substances diffuse easily between blood and tissue fluid. Thick elastic walls belong to arteries, and valves and wide lumens to veins.

questions.stem: A blood vessel has a thick wall with much elastic and muscle tissue and a narrow lumen, and the blood in it is under high pressure. Which vessel is it and why does the structure suit it?
options: An artery: elastic walls stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, withstanding high pressure
A vein: thick walls stop blood flowing backwards at the low pressure in it
A capillary: thick walls let substances exchange with the body's cells
A vein: the narrow lumen speeds blood back to the heart against gravity
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; their elastic walls stretch and recoil, smoothing the flow. Veins have thin walls, wide lumens and valves, and capillaries have walls one cell thick.

questions.stem: Why do veins in the legs have valves?
options: Blood pressure in veins is low, so valves prevent backflow
Blood pressure in veins is high, so valves reduce the pressure
Valves in veins pump blood back towards the heart by contracting
Valves in veins let oxygen diffuse out into the leg muscles
questions.explanation: By the time blood reaches the veins its pressure is low. Valves stop it flowing backwards, and contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins to push blood towards the heart. Valves do not contract themselves.

questions.stem: The circulatory system transports materials to and from several exchange surfaces. Which pairing of an organ and the exchange that happens there is correct?
options: Kidneys: oxygen is absorbed into the blood from the air
Kidneys: urea and excess water are removed from the blood
Lungs: digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood
Small intestine: carbon dioxide is removed from the blood
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter wastes such as urea and excess water from the blood. Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine, and oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves the blood in the lungs.

questions.stem: Which component of blood carries most of the oxygen?
options: White blood cells
Platelets
Plasma
Red blood cells
questions.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Very little oxygen dissolves in plasma.

questions.stem: What is the main role of platelets?
options: Engulfing and destroying bacteria
Carrying dissolved nutrients and urea
Helping blood to clot at a wound
Carrying oxygen to the body cells
questions.explanation: Platelets are cell fragments that start blood clotting, sealing wounds. Red blood cells carry oxygen, some white blood cells engulf bacteria, and plasma carries dissolved substances.

questions.stem: Which substances are carried dissolved in the plasma?
options: Platelets, white blood cells and red blood cells
Starch, proteins and fats from food that is undigested
Glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide
Haemoglobin, glucose and the nuclei of red blood cells
questions.explanation: Plasma is mostly water carrying dissolved nutrients, wastes such as urea and carbon dioxide, hormones and proteins. Blood cells and platelets are suspended in it, not dissolved, and food is digested before it is absorbed.

questions.stem: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and a biconcave disc shape. How do these features help their function?
options: A nucleus is not needed because red blood cells divide very quickly
The shape lets them squeeze into the alveoli to collect oxygen directly
The missing nucleus lets them engulf invading bacteria in the bloodstream
More room for haemoglobin and a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse
questions.explanation: Without a nucleus a red blood cell can hold more haemoglobin, and its biconcave shape gives a large surface area for oxygen to diffuse in and out. Red blood cells cannot divide, and they stay inside capillaries.

questions.stem: Which tissue carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves?
options: Xylem
Phloem
Epidermis
Stomata
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are hollow tubes of dead cells that carry water and dissolved minerals upwards. Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In plant transport, what does the term translocation mean?
options: The movement of water up the xylem from the roots
The loss of water vapour from the leaves through stomata
The movement of gases through the air spaces inside the leaf
The movement of sugars and some minerals through the phloem
questions.explanation: Translocation is the transport of the products of photosynthesis, mainly sucrose, and some mineral nutrients in the phloem, from where they are made or stored to where they are used. Loss of water vapour is transpiration.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares xylem and phloem?
options: Xylem carries sugars both up and down; phloem carries water upwards only
Xylem carries gases into the leaf; phloem carries water out of the leaf
Xylem and phloem both carry water from the roots to the leaves only
Xylem carries water upwards only; phloem carries sugars both up and down
questions.explanation: Water and minerals move one way, up the xylem from roots to leaves. Sugars in the phloem move to wherever they are needed, such as growing tips and roots, so the flow can go up or down.

questions.stem: How does transpiration help move water up the xylem?
options: Sunlight heats the water in the xylem so that it rises as vapour
Evaporation from leaves pulls a continuous column of water up from the roots
Water evaporating from roots pushes the column up towards the leaves
Phloem cells pump water into the xylem using energy from sugars
questions.explanation: Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through the stomata. This draws water out of the xylem, and because water molecules cling together (cohesion), the whole column is pulled up.

questions.stem: The stem of a small plant is cut just above the soil, and sap oozes from the cut end of the stump for some time. Which process explains this?
options: Translocation moving sugars down in the phloem
Diffusion of gases out through the stomata
Root pressure pushing water up from the roots
Transpiration pulling water up from the leaves
questions.explanation: With the leaves removed there is no transpiration pull, so sap rising from the stump must be pushed up by root pressure, which builds up as roots take in water. Translocation moves sugars, not this flow of water.

questions.stem: On which day would the rate of water movement up the xylem of a eucalypt be greatest?
options: Cool, dry, windy and dark, with stomata closed
Warm, dry, windy and sunny, with stomata open
Cool, humid, still and cloudy, with stomata open
Warm, humid, still and dark, with stomata closed
questions.explanation: Warmth, low humidity, wind and light (which keeps stomata open) all increase evaporation from the leaves, so transpiration and the pull on the xylem are greatest. With stomata closed, little water vapour can escape.
